practicalQuestion: When symptoms and clinic-based measures have normalized but high-speed and sport-specific exposure remain incomplete, how should physical therapy and performance staff structure the next 7–10 days and define progress, hold, or regress criteria without relying on a single return-to-sport cutoff?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete nearing unrestricted participation after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.sport: Field sport with sprinting, cutting, and reactive demands
decisionContext.phase: Modified participation to unrestricted team activity
decisionContext.outcome: Coordinate staged exposure and decision ownership across rehabilitation and performance staff
decisionContext.constraints: Limited practice opportunities; competition schedule continues; no athlete-identifying or diagnosis-specific data

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source tests a 7 to 10 day structure or validated progress, hold, or regress rules for this situation. The closest direct evidence is one case series and one single case in male soccer after ACL reconstruction. Other sources are hamstring-specific, observational, survey, or editorial evidence from professional settings.

dimensions.sourceReview: Three sources were full-text screened (libraryId 705, 212 via digest abstract, 683). The ACL case report, practice survey, and deceleration editorial are legacy records not full-text reviewed.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. The sources describe staged on-field loads, near-maximal speed timing, and practice patterns. None compares structured late-stage plans or tests hold or regress triggers.
dimensions.consistency: Broadly consistent that staged field work and planned high-speed exposure matter and that staff use several criteria. The evidence is too thin to judge consistency on any specific criterion.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Populations were male amateur and professional soccer players after ACL reconstruction, elite European professional soccer teams, professional male footballers, and Brazilian elite club physical therapists. No collegiate, female, or mixed lower-extremity injury samples were included.

bottomLine.text: The library has no tested 7 to 10 day protocol or validated progress, hold, or regress criteria for this situation. In male soccer players after ACL reconstruction, staged on-field work approached team training loads but stayed below match demands, especially for deceleration. Total distance plateaued, and the authors judged it not useful for progression decisions. Practitioners in one survey combined several criteria rather than one cutoff.

actions.title: Option: plan the week around metric-by-metric gaps
actions.text: One option is to compare recent field outputs with team training and match references for each metric separately, such as high-intensity distance, peak speed, acceleration, and deceleration. Staff could then target the largest gaps. In the ACL case series, final-stage outputs met or exceeded team training on some metrics but not others, and none reached match demands. Total distance was judged not useful for progression. The evidence does not test a specific 7 to 10 day sequence.

actions.title: Option: give deceleration exposure specific attention
actions.text: Deceleration distance was the lowest final-stage output relative to both team training and match play in the ACL case series. An editorial argues deceleration is often overlooked in rehabilitation. This is a reason to consider deliberate deceleration and cutting exposure. It is not a tested progression rule.

actions.title: Option: choose where near-maximal speed falls in the competition week
actions.text: In elite professional soccer, no match hamstring injuries occurred when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed fell two days before a match. Injuries did occur when players had no such exposure. Staff could consider placing near-maximal speed work two days before competition or choose another day based on local recovery patterns. This was a retrospective association in healthy players for hamstring injuries only, and the authors note the optimal dose is likely population-specific.

actions.title: Option: use a multi-criteria panel with named owners
actions.text: Practitioners in one survey combined strength, sprint or high-speed running, intense actions, pain, and GPS workload when releasing athletes to team training. A single case report describes return to sport as a gradual transition from rehabilitation to performance. Step impulse asymmetry is proposed there as one input to phase progression. The evidence does not test who should own each decision. Agreeing in advance which clinician or coach owns each criterion is professional caution, not an evidence-based finding.

monitoring.label: Exposure versus reference demands
monitoring.text: Track high-intensity distance, peak speed, acceleration, and deceleration against team training and match references. Do not rely on total distance alone.

monitoring.label: Weekly near-maximal efforts and strength response
monitoring.text: In 58 professional male footballers, weekly sprint distance and weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity showed inverse relationships with eccentric hamstring strength change (rho -0.13 and -0.08). Tracking weekly near-maximal efforts alongside a strength measure is an option. These were healthy players, and the study did not test return-to-sport decisions.

monitoring.label: Between-limb asymmetry
monitoring.text: One single case report proposes step impulse asymmetry, tracked throughout rehabilitation, as an input to phase progression. It is a single-case suggestion, not a validated threshold.

guardrails.text: This brief informs professional judgment only. Progression, hold, regress, and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians. Practice varies, and no single criterion in this evidence defines readiness.
Do not treat completion of staged field work as equivalent to match readiness. Final-stage loads in the ACL case series remained below match play demands.
Do not present the two-days-before-match timing of near-maximal speed as proven protection. It is a retrospective, hamstring-specific association in elite professional soccer.

The evidence does not test specific hold or regress triggers. Any triggers staff use, such as symptom response or missed exposure targets, are local professional judgments and should be labeled that way.

limitations.text: No collegiate or female athletes were studied. Direct evidence comes from male amateur and professional soccer players after ACL reconstruction and one professional soccer case. The other sources involve professional soccer and hamstring injury.
Designs are weak for decision rules. They are a level 4 case series, a single case report, a retrospective association study, a practitioner survey, and an editorial.
No source tests a 7 to 10 day structure, a congested competition schedule during return, or shared decision ownership between rehabilitation and performance staff.

whatCouldChange.text: Cohort or trial data in collegiate field-sport athletes testing staged return-to-team criteria with explicit hold or regress rules would allow a firmer direction.
Validated deceleration measures with reference values could turn deceleration from a cautious focus into a usable criterion.
Studies of near-maximal speed timing in athletes returning from injury, rather than healthy players, would show whether the two-days-before-match pattern transfers.

claims.text: In a level 4 case series of 100 male amateur and professional soccer players completing a 5-stage on-field rehabilitation program after ACL reconstruction, 97 players were followed for at least 9 months. Of these, 84% returned to competition, with higher rates in professionals (100%) than amateurs (80%).

evidence.excerpt: A minimum 9-month follow-up was possible for 97 players (97%), with a median time of 2.3 years after ACLR and 84% RTC, with higher rates in professionals (100%) than amateurs (80%).
Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods: OFR measurements/activities, global positioning system (GPS), and heart rate data were collected from 100 male

claims.text: In that case series, completing all five on-field rehabilitation stages almost prepared players for team training demands, but workloads remained low compared with match play.

evidence.excerpt: Completion of all five OFR stages almost prepared them for team training demands; however, workloads remain low compared to match play.

claims.text: Relative to team training demands, final-stage outputs in that case series were 106% for total distance, 104% for high-intensity distance, 88% for peak speed, 110% for acceleration distance, and 48% for deceleration distance. Relative to match play, they were 44%, 51%, 82%, 63%, and 26%.

but they were lower compared with match play demands (TD: 44%; HID: 51%; PS: 82%; ACC: 63%; and DEC: 26%).

claims.text: An editorial commentary summarized in a research digest argues that deceleration is a key but often overlooked part of rehabilitation. It also notes the deceleration index is still in its early stages of development.

evidence.excerpt: The ability to decelerate is a key component of any successful rehabilitation program, yet it is often overlooked in favor of more traditional forms of rehabilitation and training.
While the deceleration index is still in its early stages of development, there is promising evidence that it could be the missing link in effective rehabilitation.

claims.text: In retrospective data from 36 team-seasons of elite European professional soccer (627 players, 96 match hamstring injuries), no match hamstring injuries occurred when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before the match. Injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all.

evidence.excerpt: irrespective of the turnaround length, there were no match hamstring injuries when > 95% MSS exposures occurred at D-2, while in contrast, injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all
Retrospective data from 36 team-seasons (16 elite teams performing in top European leagues) were analyzed (627 players, 96 non-contact time loss match hamstring injuries).

evidence.excerpt: Weekly sprint distance (ρ = −0.13, p < 0.01) and weekly efforts >90% of maximum velocity (ρ = −0.08, p = 0.01) both displayed significant inverse relationships with the percentage change in eccentric hamstring strength
Fifty-eight professional male footballers were observed over one-and-a-half seasons.

assumptions: The specific lower-extremity injury is not stated, so ACL and hamstring evidence was treated as indirect rather than diagnosis-matched.
Staff were assumed to have GPS or similar field tracking to compare outputs with training and match references.
The competition schedule was assumed to follow roughly weekly matches, so match-week timing evidence was treated as potentially relevant.
coverageGaps: No study tests a structured 7 to 10 day late-stage plan or compares alternative weekly structures.
No validated progress, hold, or regress criteria for the transition from modified to unrestricted team activity.
No collegiate, female, or non-soccer field-sport samples in the direct return-to-sport evidence.
No evidence on decision ownership or coordination models between rehabilitation and performance staff.
No evidence on managing late-stage exposure while a competition schedule continues with limited practices.
Accessible text was missing for possibly relevant leads, including libraryId 614 (strength and power training in rehabilitation) and 583 (landing biomechanics after ACL reconstruction).
